questions.stem: The left ventricle has a much thicker muscular wall than the right ventricle. What is the reason for this?

options.text: The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, which are far away
The left ventricle pumps blood to the entire body, requiring higher pressure than the right ventricle which only pumps to the nearby lungs
The left ventricle contains more blood than the right
The left ventricle pumps blood faster

questions.explanation: The left ventricle must generate enough pressure to push blood through the systemic circulation -- around the entire body and back. The right ventricle only needs to push blood the short distance to the lungs. Thicker muscle walls allow stronger contractions and higher blood pressure. If the right ventricle wall were as thick, it could damage the delicate lung capillaries.

questions.stem: The heart has valves between the atria and ventricles (atrioventricular valves) and between the ventricles and arteries (semilunar valves). What is their function?

options.text: To control the speed of blood flow
To prevent the backflow of blood, ensuring blood flows in one direction only
To mix oxygenated and deoxygenated blood
To filter impurities from the blood

questions.explanation: Heart valves are one-way doors that open under pressure to allow blood through, then close to prevent backflow. The atrioventricular valves (bicuspid and tricuspid) prevent blood flowing back from ventricles to atria. Semilunar valves prevent blood flowing back from arteries into the ventricles. Valve defects cause heart murmurs.

questions.stem: The coronary arteries supply blood to the heart muscle itself. If a coronary artery becomes blocked by a blood clot, what happens?

options.text: The heart receives too much blood
Part of the heart muscle is deprived of oxygen and may die, causing a heart attack (myocardial infarction)
Blood pressure decreases immediately
The heart switches to anaerobic respiration permanently

questions.explanation: The heart muscle needs a constant supply of oxygen and glucose (delivered by coronary arteries) for aerobic respiration to produce the ATP needed for continuous contraction. A blocked coronary artery starves the heart muscle of oxygen, causing cells to die. This is a heart attack, which can be fatal if a large area of muscle is affected.

questions.stem: A diagram of the heart shows four chambers. A student labels the right side on their left when looking at the diagram. Why does the heart appear 'the wrong way round' in diagrams?

options.text: The diagram is drawn incorrectly
Heart diagrams show the heart as if looking at someone facing you, so the right side appears on your left
The heart is in the centre of the chest so left and right do not apply
The left and right sides are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Heart diagrams are drawn from the patient's perspective (or as if you are facing someone). This means the patient's right side appears on your left, and vice versa. This is standard anatomical convention. The right side of the heart (which receives deoxygenated blood) appears on the left side of the diagram.

questions.stem: The septum is a thick wall of muscle that separates the left and right sides of the heart. Why is it essential that oxygenated and deoxygenated blood do not mix?

options.text: Mixing would cause the blood to clot
Mixing would reduce the oxygen concentration of blood going to the body, making oxygen delivery to tissues less efficient
Mixing would increase blood pressure dangerously
Mixing would destroy red blood cells

questions.explanation: If oxygenated blood from the lungs mixed with deoxygenated blood returning from the body, the resulting blood would have a lower oxygen concentration. This would reduce the amount of oxygen delivered to body tissues, meaning cells would receive insufficient oxygen for aerobic respiration. The septum ensures fully oxygenated blood is pumped to the body.
